fabrications.carrier_title: Product page: Speckled Buff Stoneware, Cone 10
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Speckled Buff is a high-fire stoneware body formulated for wheel throwing and functional ware. It fires to a warm toasted buff in reduction, with fine iron speckles that bleed through light glazes for a natural, earthy surface. In oxidation it fires a lighter cream with softer speckling.

The body contains a moderate amount of fine grog, which gives it good standing strength for tall forms without feeling rough on the hands. Plasticity is high enough for pulling handles and trimming thin feet.

{INJECTION}

Technical data: firing range cone 9 to 11. Total shrinkage around 12 percent at cone 10. Absorption below 1.5 percent at cone 10 reduction, making it suitable for tableware and mugs. Supplied in 25 kg boxes containing two sealed 12.5 kg bags. Store bags out of direct sunlight and away from frost. Pairs well with celadons, shinos and tenmoku glazes. Sample bags are available for testing before ordering in bulk.

fabrications.carrier_title: Dust Safety in the Glaze Room
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Glaze materials are mostly harmless once fired, but in raw powder form many of them pose real health risks. Silica, the main glass-former in most recipes, can cause permanent lung damage when inhaled over many years. Some colourants, such as manganese and barium compounds, carry their own hazards.

The biggest single improvement most studios can make is to stop sweeping. Dry sweeping lifts fine dust into the air where it stays for hours. Wet mopping or a vacuum with a proper HEPA filter is far safer.

{INJECTION}

Wear a fitted respirator rated for fine particulates whenever you weigh or mix dry materials, not a paper dust mask. Mix glazes in a dedicated area away from where you eat or wedge clay. Keep lids on buckets and label every container with its contents and the date. Wash work clothes separately and often. Finally, make sure your kiln room is vented, because firing releases fumes from glazes and clay bodies that should not build up indoors.

fabrications.carrier_title: Forum thread: Silicon carbide or cordierite kiln shelves?
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Original post: My old cordierite shelves are starting to warp after years of cone 10 reduction firing. Is it worth paying for silicon carbide, or should I just replace like for like?

Reply 1: I switched to nitride-bonded silicon carbide five years ago and haven't looked back. They're thinner and lighter, so I fit an extra layer in the kiln, and none have sagged.

Reply 2: Silicon carbide conducts heat better, so the bottom of pots heats more evenly. I noticed fewer dunting cracks on wide platters after switching.

{INJECTION}

Reply 3: Be careful in reduction. Some silicon carbide shelves can bloat or oxidize over time if the kiln atmosphere is heavy. Ask the supplier which grade is rated for reduction.

Reply 4: Whatever you buy, keep kiln wash on top only, never on the underside, or it flakes onto the pots below. And flip cordierite shelves every firing if you stay with them, which slows the warping a lot.

fabrications.carrier_title: Ten Small Changes That Made My Studio Easier to Work In
fabrications.carrier_doc:
After twelve years in the same studio, I finally took a weekend to rethink how the space works. None of these changes cost much, but together they saved me hours every month.

First, I moved the wedging table next to the wheel so I stopped carrying clay across the room. Second, I put every glaze bucket on a rolling dolly, which ended the back strain from lifting them. Third, I added a pegboard above the wheel for trimming tools, ribs and sponges.

{INJECTION}

Fourth, I installed a second sink trap to catch clay before it reaches the drain. Fifth, I bought ware boards cut to fit my shelves exactly. Sixth, I hung a clock where I can see it from the wheel. Seventh, I put an extension cord reel by the kiln for the vent fan. Eighth, I swapped my stool for one with adjustable height. Ninth, I added task lighting over the glazing table. Tenth, I cleared one shelf just for finished work waiting for photography.

fabrications.carrier_title: Product page: Professional Pottery Wheel, 1/2 HP
fabrications.carrier_doc:
Our professional wheel is built for potters who throw every day. A half horsepower motor delivers steady torque from a slow crawl to 250 rpm, handling up to 45 kg of clay without stalling. The direct-drive system has no belts to wear or slip, and it runs almost silently.

The cast aluminium wheel head measures 35 cm and includes bat pins at standard spacing. A one-piece splash pan lifts off for cleaning in seconds.

{INJECTION}

The foot pedal has a smooth, progressive response and a cruise control setting that holds speed while you trim. A reversing switch makes the wheel suitable for left-handed throwers. Adjustable leg extensions let you raise the wheel by up to 15 cm for standing work. Every wheel comes with a ten-year warranty on the motor and a two-year warranty on the electronics. Shipping is free within the mainland, and the wheel arrives fully assembled and ready to use.
